title: Between a Rock and a Hard Place: Critical Thinking and Persuasive Writing
author: Terry Yu
summary: Terry Yu subjects the foundational assumption of academic writing pedagogy — that persuasive essay assignments develop critical thinking — to rigorous critical analysis and finds it far less secure than it appears. Drawing on Janet Emig and seminal writing researchers, Yu explains what writing distinctively does: it externalizes thought, making the sentence an inspectable object that the writer can interrogate, contradict, and rebuild in a recursive produce-inspect-revise loop mostly unavailable in real-time speech. Speaking is thinking in motion — irreversible, linear, and shaped by an interlocutor's resistance in ways writing's typically monologic form cannot replicate. Yu then interrogates the persuasive essay genre specifically: it requires students to argue for a predetermined position, which may suppress critical thinking by incentivizing the marshaling of evidence for a conclusion already reached rather than genuine inquiry toward an uncertain one. AI-generated text enters as a case study: Yu argues it is closer to speech than writing — produced without the reflective revision loop that makes writing constitutive of thought — and therefore a poor model of critical thinking despite its surface coherence. The practical implication for educators is that tasks requiring genuine inquiry under uncertainty produce more authentic critical thinking than tasks requiring performed advocacy.
points: Writing's critical-thinking value derives from the externalization loop: a sentence on the page becomes an object the writer can inspect, contradict, and rebuild — a recursive process of produce-inspect-revise that is the mechanism by which writing constitutes thought rather than merely expressing it.

Speaking is thinking in motion rather than thinking-then-reporting: the irreversibility of spoken language and the real-time pressure of an interlocutor surface different cognitive processes — forward-moving, dialogically shaped, generating surprises through the constraints of real-time production.

Persuasive essays may suppress the critical thinking they are designed to develop: the genre rewards marshaling evidence for a predetermined conclusion rather than genuine inquiry toward an uncertain one, training students in advocacy rather than in analysis.

AI-generated text is closer to speech than writing by Yu's analysis: produced without the reflective revision loop, synthetic text is generated rather than composed, making it a poor model of critical thinking despite its surface-level rhetorical coherence.

The implication for curriculum design is that genuine critical thinking requires tasks with open inquiry rather than performed advocacy: students must confront real uncertainty, weigh genuinely competing evidence, and have reason to revise their initial position rather than defend it.
quotes: We know that writing is thinking. For that reason, writing is a staple assignment in academic classrooms.

There’s also the interlocutor. Speaking is usually thinking with someone, not just thinking. A conversation partner interrupts, pushes back, asks a real-time question you didn’t anticipate — the thought gets shaped by resistance from another mind, which is dialogic while writing is too often monologic, leaving little space for a reader.

When I first read this study almost two decades ago, I explained this finding of misalignment between assignment design and expected outcome as a function of what teachers usually teach students about when and how a thesis statement gets written and begins to govern the text. The moment the thesis appears in the writing process, the writer shifts from critical thinking to making an artifact.

The first assignment can probably be gamed by an AI. A student could collect a set of documents from the Office of Institutional Research which likely has records from student satisfaction surveys. A search of the student newspaper, also online, can provide local color and detail.
Above all, Bloom was after a construct of higher-order thinking that could be measured on a mass scale.

That embeddedness and embodiedness is not incidental; it is constitutive of the thinking itself. WSU’s treats context and assumptions as separate dimensions requiring active engagement, dimensions that demand a situated thinker, not merely a processor of verbal representations. The difference between a critical thinker and a critical thinker-in-context is fundamental.
